title: Tomorrow’s market today: Why Europe needs to invest in AI compute – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Prokopiev argues Europe cannot match US AI capex but should build an exchange-traded compute price index and power-plus-compute contract, so banks can finance EU data centres and Europe is not a price-taker on a CME-set benchmark.

insights.claim: In 2025 a megawatt-hour of European wholesale electricity cost about $95, while running it through the newest AI chips rented at Amazon list prices would earn about $8,540, roughly 90 times the electricity cost.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Explains why power-secured data-centre capacity is attractive.

insights.claim: Bruegel estimates the EU has about 5% of world AI compute in 2026 versus 78% for the US, and the EU's InvestAI plan of EUR 200bn is about a third of the more than $700bn Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta spend this year.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev

insights.claim: CME Group planned to start compute futures on October 5th but the US regulator extended its review to November 9th, and Intercontinental Exchange is preparing similar contracts.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Compute derivatives launch is a near-term catalyst; watch November 9th.

insights.claim: Whoever sets the official price tends to dominate a market, as London still clears over 90% of euro interest-rate swaps despite post-Brexit EU efforts, so a Chicago compute benchmark would be hard to dislodge.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Benchmark first-mover advantage implies value for early compute-index operators.

insights.claim: Amazon, Microsoft and Google hold around 70% of Europe's cloud market, so Europe dependent on America for chips, cloud and compute price has little leverage in trade talks.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler dependence is a geopolitical vulnerability.
insights.quote: A Europe that depends on America for chips, cloud and the price of compute has little leverage left in trade and technology talks

insights.claim: Banks cannot finance European data centres because compute is sold in private deals with no benchmark for three-year earnings, unlike wind farms that borrow against power contracts priced off liquid exchanges.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: A public compute price would unlock project finance for EU data centres.

insights.claim: The plan: a European compute index published by existing power exchanges, then a standardised power-plus-compute contract, with political commitment by end-2026, a pilot index in 2027 and a full contract by 2028 under the Cloud and AI Development Act and ESMA supervision.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Timeline for possible new EU commodity-like market.

insights.claim: To seed liquidity, the EU could require publicly supported data centres, including gigafactories, to sell part of their capacity on the market, and the EIB could provide first-loss guarantees, which it has not yet committed to.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Public backstops could de-risk compute-linked lending.

insights.claim: Chip rents fall with each Nvidia annual generation, so contracts cannot copy 15-year wind PPAs, but separate indices per chip generation and shorter contracts let lenders model rent decay.
insights.speaker: Ivo Prokopiev
insights.so_what: Chip depreciation is the core credit risk for compute-backed debt.
